prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I ranked the KPZ ballot (B005) first on scientific grounds, and I still think it is an excellent candidate. Reading the opening ballots, however, I do not find that it can carry a prize in this committee: it has only my support, and the credit problem (exact-solution contributors and Parisi are outside the credited names) is real. The optical lattice clock (B040) is the candidate where the scientific case and the committee evidence coincide. Seven of eight members ranked it, six place it in their top three, and all seven who propose laureates name the same pair. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the conflict between trapping many atoms and keeping the clock transition unperturbed, and Ye's group took the platform to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The result is a concrete invention with confirmed, independently reproduced performance, and it is the basis for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the expected redefinition of the second. The two-name credit is clean, which is rare on this shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness from earlier precision-measurement prizes: the 2005 prize covered the optical frequency comb (with Ye's group a major user and developer) and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, which underlie the competing ion clocks. A committee could read the lattice clock as the natural continuation of those awards rather than a separate discovery. There are also contributors (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hollberg and others) outside the two credited names, and part of the impact, namely the redefinition of the second, is still prospective. I judge these concerns real but not decisive, because the lattice-clock concept and its record accuracy are separable and specific.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B040 first as an advance in what can be measured and how accurately, and sees it as timely and arguably overdue relative to Wineland and Hall.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this, and it is why I move B040 to the head of my configuration. I am less comfortable with 'overdue relative to Wineland/Hall': that argument leans on prize history and could be turned around, since it is exactly the overlap that the committee will be asked about. The better argument is the one Kroll also makes, that the magic-wavelength idea is a distinct invention. Where I differ from Kroll is B010. I ranked QKD sixth because I regard it as a protocol-level contribution with a heavier overlap with the 2022 prize than Kroll allows, and I would not put it above B040 or B061.

responses.point: Lindroth, as an atomic physicist, sees a single coherent story in B040 with a clean two-name credit, and considers it distinct enough from the comb and ion-clock prizes because the clocks now beat microwave standards by orders of magnitude.
responses.response: I accept her assessment of attribution and of maturity. My one qualification concerns the uncertainty she herself raises, the relative contributions of Katori and Ye to the later accuracy records. The committee should word the citation around the invention and development of the clock, not around the record numbers, so that the laureates are credited for the concept and the platform and not for a specific figure that other groups are also improving. I do not share her ranking of the Cirac-Zoller-Blatt ballot (B032) second: I think the two-theorist version (B004) is cleaner than adding Blatt, though I take her point that Wineland and Monroe then become the obvious omissions.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the topological-insulator ballot (B061) second and notes that the 2016 prize on topological phases and the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit weigh against it, while placing B040 only fifth because of the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I share the concern about B061 and ranked it fourth for the same reasons: the 2016 prize and the omission of BHZ make a three-name award contestable, and Zhang's death rules him out in any case. I disagree with Eriksson's discount of B040 for prize-history overlap. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb, and the 2012 prize rewarded ion control, while the lattice clock rests on a different physical idea, namely trapping at a magic wavelength so that the lattice does not shift the transition. If overlap with a neighbouring prize is disqualifying, the same argument weakens B061 more than B040, because B061 is adjacent to a prize in the same condensed-matter subject.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B018) first as a genuinely new instrument that opened neutrino astronomy, while accepting that the origin of most of the diffuse flux is unresolved.
responses.response: The instrumental achievement is impressive and the diffuse flux is established, but I weigh the maturity differently. The source identification rests on a few associations, and the dominant origin is open, so the citation would have to describe a detection of a flux rather than a result with a settled interpretation. Only four members ranked B018, and one of them put it seventh. I would hold it in reserve until the source picture is firmer, and I do not think it should compete with B040 for this year's prize. If the committee did choose it, the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage would need explicit mention in the citation.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B055) first for its originality and for its role as the architecture of superconducting processors, and flags a possible conflict from his own proximity to the field.
responses.response: I respect the scientific case and his disclosure. My reservation is the one he states himself: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits makes it hard to present cQED as a separate achievement so soon, and Girvin and Devoret-side contributions are missing from the credited names. With only two members ranking B055, the evidence for a prize this year is thin. I would sooner see his support go to a candidate where the committee can argue the case without that overlap.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and how the citation should word that distinction.
The relative weight of Katori and Ye against other lattice-clock groups (for example Lemonde, Ludlow, Hollberg) cannot be resolved from the supplied credit.
Part of the clock's claimed impact, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, so the measurement-science argument is partly prospective.
Whether my own first-ranked candidate (B005, KPZ) could build committee support in a later round once the exact-solution credit problem is discussed; at present I do not think it can.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B040, B005, B004 or B061. I note scientific proximity rather than a personal connection: B005 lies in my own field of stochastic processes and random matrices, which is why I disclose it, and none of my listed co-authors or institutions appear among the credited names for the preferred configuration.
